headline: AWS can be a $1T business, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy says, but requires massive investment
summary: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy reiterated his belief that AWS can achieve $1 trillion in annual revenue. However, this goal necessitates substantial capital expenditure, with Amazon planning to spend approximately $220 billion by 2026, mostly on AWS AI infrastructure.
details: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has publicly stated his ambition for AWS to become a trillion-dollar annual revenue business. To achieve this, Amazon plans a significant increase in capital expenditures, projecting approximately $220 billion in cash capex by 2026, with the majority allocated to AWS.

This massive investment is primarily directed towards building out the necessary AI infrastructure to support the burgeoning cloud business. Jassy emphasized that the company expects to spend "meaningfully more" in 2027, with clear sight of attractive financial returns.

Investors have expressed concerns regarding Amazon's substantial spending on AI infrastructure. Wall Street analysts questioned Jassy during the recent earnings call about the rationale, expected growth signals, and profit margins.

Jassy defended the investment, characterizing the AI boom as a "once in a lifetime opportunity" that demands such a large financial commitment. He stated that AWS is currently an $184 billion annualized revenue run-rate business.

The CEO forecasts AWS to grow "north of 40 percent" in both 2027 and 2028, driven by continued innovation, new core and AI functionality, and enterprises migrating workloads to AWS. He believes the strategy is working, despite a 6% dip in shares post-earnings.

The AI boom has led to increased spending across the cloud industry. Other major cloud providers, such as Microsoft, are also investing heavily in infrastructure to support AI services, while simultaneously reporting record-breaking revenue growth in their cloud segments.

headline_marked: [[Intel is selling every affordable laptop chip it can make]] as demand outstrips supply
headline: Intel is selling every affordable laptop chip it can make as demand outstrips supply
summary: Demand for its budget-focused Wildcat Lake chips is outstripping supply, even as Intel warns that memory shortages will persist through 2027, impacting PC prices and availability.
details: Intel's CFO David Zinsner announced that demand for its budget-focused Wildcat Lake chips is currently outstripping supply, with the chips now completely sold out. CEO Lip-Bu Tan noted the significant growth in Wildcat Lake, calling it "cost-optimized" and arriving at the right time for the market.

These Wildcat Lake chips are featured in new lower-cost Windows laptops, such as the Dell XPS 13 and HP Omnibook 5 14, offering budget-friendly starting prices. This comes as recent shortages of RAM and other components have driven up overall PC prices.

Despite the strong demand for its affordable chips, Intel is not optimistic about the memory market for the coming year. Zinsner stated that memory shortages are expected to continue through 2027, with potential improvements only by 2028, a more positive outlook than SK Hynix's prediction of shortages until 2030.

Tan also acknowledged a broader slowdown in PC demand, attributing it to "unprecedented demand for super intelligence," referring to AI. However, Zinsner maintains a positive long-term outlook, believing the PC industry will undergo a "renaissance" despite current challenges.
